claims.text: Adding 0.5–1 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 is the proposed intervention.
Enhanced dispersion techniques will produce a uniform Y2O3 nanoparticle distribution before consolidation.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles preferentially absorb irradiation-induced vacancies.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles preferentially absorb irradiation-induced interstitials.
Point-defect absorption by Y2O3 nanoparticles lowers the concentration of free irradiation-induced defects.
Lowering the free point-defect concentration reduces local solute supersaturation.
Reduced local solute supersaturation suppresses radiation-induced precipitate nucleation.
At approximately 8 dpa, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have about 50% less precipitate volume fraction than the unmodified alloy.
At approximately 8 dpa, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have a lower irradiation-induced defect density than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening.
The Y2O3 dispersion will improve the alloy's suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits radiation-induced precipitation at approximately 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 presents processing challenges for bulk applications.
Irradiation with 1–5 MeV particles to approximately 8 dpa at 600–800 °C is representative of fusion-relevant service conditions.
The proposed intervention is applicable up to approximately 8 dpa within the temperature range 600–800 °C.
Oxide dispersoids are known to produce the predicted effects in similar material systems.

contradictions.description: The material_initial_state already includes a pre-engineered Y2O3 dispersion, whereas the intervention describes introducing that dispersion into the starting alloy and the baseline identifies the starting alloy as unmodified.

The hypothesis requires both precipitation suppression and retention of negligible hardening, but the falsification rule requires both the precipitation target and hardening behavior to fail simultaneously. Failure of either essential prediction alone would therefore not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
